prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration I stated in round 1: the optical lattice clock (B008), credited to Katori and Ye. Having read all eight statements and the chair's summary, I find that the case rests on substance and not on the support count. The invention is specific: a magic-wavelength optical lattice that cancels Doppler, recoil and first-order light shifts while many neutral atoms are interrogated in parallel. That combination is what moved optical clocks from the 1e-16 regime to about 1e-18, and it is not delivered by a frequency comb, which is a counting tool, or by single-ion control, which gives one particle. The performance is independently reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg, and the consequences are physical and not only technical: clock comparisons that resolve gravitational redshift over centimetre-scale height differences, tight limits on drifting constants, and the basis for the planned redefinition of the second. Katori's proposal and first demonstrations and Ye's record accuracy and many-body operation form a two-name allocation with no arbitrary cut. As to the chair's first question, I would draft the citation on the lattice clock itself, as above, and I would say nothing in it about the SI second or timekeeping in general.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is still distinctness from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. Danielsson and Olsson regard this as open, and Mehlig correctly says the overlap argument is not unique to B008. I judge it answered, because neutral-atom lattice interrogation is a different physical idea from either precedent, but a sceptical Academy member could read the clock as the culmination of an already honoured line, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser background makes that reading easier. The second objection is credit: the NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo groups, early lattice-clock proposals and the ion-clock community lie outside the two names, and I think the committee has to accept that a two-name prize cannot cover the field. Third, the pending SI redefinition cuts both ways. I do not think it is a reason to wait, but I cannot claim it is irrelevant to how the prize will be read.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps trapped-ion quantum logic (B022) as the preferred prize, concedes that the experimental share is contestable because of Wineland's NIST group and Monroe, and says the overlap argument against B022 applies equally to B008.
responses.response: The symmetry point is fair and I do not dismiss it. Both entries sit near earlier prizes. The difference I still see is in what the overlap touches. The 2012 prize recognised control of individual trapped quantum systems, and the first ion entangling gates came out of exactly that NIST work, so the experimental half of B022 is partly inside recognised territory and the third name remains a judgment call, as you concede. The lattice clock is a different mechanism, a neutral-atom ensemble at a magic wavelength, and nothing in 2005 or 2012 describes it. I agree with you that the Cirac and Zoller proposal is a conceptual advance of the first order, and I rank B022 as my second alternative for that reason. If the committee wanted a quantum-information prize, I would support Cirac and Zoller, but I could not defend a prize whose experimental credit we cannot allocate in this room. Your own statement that B008 is the more compact prize if those points are unresolved is the conclusion I draw.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene (B035) on scientific weight, arguing that a tunable correlated-electron platform changes how we understand matter more than a precision gain does, and holds that the prize can precede a settled mechanism.
responses.response: I accept the principle that we have honoured discoveries before their mechanism was understood, and the prediction-plus-discovery structure of B035 is attractive. I disagree on the weight argument. A clock at 1e-18 is not only a better ruler: it makes gravitational time dilation measurable across a laboratory, and it tests whether fundamental constants drift, which is a statement about physics and not about instruments. On maturity, your concession about Cao and the other experimental groups matters to me more than the mechanism debate, because the three-name set would leave out the people who did much of the 2018 experimental work. I would want the pairing mechanism debate and the experimental credit to settle further. I also note that you list B008 as your first alternative and call it entirely defensible, so we differ about priority and not about whether the clock is a sound prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B008 first, judges that precedent does not weaken it because the 2005 prize rewarded comb-based measurement and the lattice clock is a different trapping and interrogation idea, and finds no two-part pairing stronger than the clock alone.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and with your reading of precedent, and I accept your point that no pairing improves on the clock alone; I tried the combinations I could think of and each one adds a credit dispute or a maturity question without adding scientific weight. I would add one thing on the disclosure you made. Your stay in Hall's laboratory is on the 2005 side of the comparison, so if anything it makes you a well informed judge of the distinctness question, and I see no reason to discount your reasoning, though it should stay in the minutes. Where I would qualify you is that the citation should avoid the word 'accuracy' as the thing being rewarded. The point is the invention of the lattice architecture, with the accuracy as its demonstrated result.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B008 but holds that the committee must say explicitly why the lattice architecture is a distinct invention, would not widen the credit to comb or ultrastable-laser contributors, and would sooner see the Higgs experimental discovery than IceCube as a second part.
responses.response: I accept your request that the citation carry the distinction, and I think the words 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' do so by naming the lattice. I also agree that widening the credit to the comb and ultrastable-laser communities would blur it. On a second part, I do not support adding the Higgs discovery. I do not doubt its scientific weight, and you are right that the discovery is the larger event. But my objection is the same one Kroll, Olsson and Pearce raised: any three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is an arbitrary cut, you and Olsson proposed different three-name sets, and I cannot judge the large-collaboration conventions as a theorist. A two-part prize that adds a disputed allocation to a clean one is weaker than the clean one alone, so I would hold the Higgs for a year in which the committee has agreed a principle for naming individuals.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the citation say plainly that the prize is for the invention and its realisation at extreme accuracy and not for the whole field of optical clocks, and that her own first choice B009 is in her field, so she would consider recusal on it.
responses.response: I agree with the drafting request and have written the citation accordingly. It names the lattice clock and its development, and it does not say optical clocks, optical timekeeping or the second. I also respect your candour on B009. Since your preference is already B008, I do not think the question of recusal arises for the lead configuration, and I see no reason for any discount of your reasoning on B008. On B009 itself, I read the Krivanek and independent STEM-corrector problem as you do: it leaves a real attribution hole, and I would not put it ahead of a pair with no comparable hole.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; I judge it answered but others do not.

Whether Katori and Ye adequately carry the credit given the NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo contributions; this is a judgment and not a verifiable fact, and the priority details between the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations I recall from memory.
How the pending redefinition of the SI second will colour the reception of the prize, in either direction.
Whether a second circuit-related prize could ever be defended so soon after 2025; I think B012 is distinct but I would not press it.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. I am director of WACQT at Chalmers, a close colleague of Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, a frequent co-author with Anton Frisk Kockum, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. These ties bear on circuit QED (B012) and superconducting-circuit work generally. Because B012 is no longer my preferred configuration and no member leads with it, I do not see a recusal question for the vote I propose, but I would recuse on B012 if it became a leading candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B008, where I note that the other disclosures in the chair's summary (Kroll's link to Hall's laboratory, Olsson on B009, Pearce on B042) do not touch Katori or Ye personally. I apply no discount to those members' views on B008 beyond what they have stated.
